Below is a high-level overview of the kinds of materials and production steps that are used in the commercial/central-bank printing of banknotes—and which, when mimicked on a smaller scale, yield very detailed “replica” or “prop” notes.  This is intended purely as background on industrial printing technologies and substrates; any attempt to reproduce legal tender without authorization is illegal.

1. Substrate (Paper or Polymer)  
 • Cotton-linen blend paper (typically 75 % cotton/25 % linen)  
 • Fully synthetic polymer films (e.g. biaxially oriented polypropylene)  
 • Key treatments: surface sizing (to control ink spread), calcium carbonate fill (for opacity), anti-static and antifungal coatings  

2. Security Threads & Windows  
 • Embedded metallic or polymer threads (woven or windowed pattern)  
 • Clear polymer “windows” or inlays in polymer notes  
 • Micro-optical elements (e.g. micro-lens films that animate a stripe when tilted)  

3. Inks & Pigments  
 • Intaglio inks (very viscous, oil-based, high-relief)  
 • Offset litho inks (water-based or UV-curable for fine four-colour backgrounds)  
 • Magnetic and infrared-responsive pigments (for machine authentication)  
 • Optically variable (colour-shifting) pigments and holographic foils  
 • Fluorescent additives (UV visible)  

4. Plate-making & Image Carriers  
 • Steel engraving (roll or flat plates) for intaglio: designs are die-sunk into steel and then chemically or mechanically textured for micro-relief  
 • Photopolymer or rubber plates for offset and letterpress  
 • Laser-engraved cylinders for screen printing of security inks or varnishes  

5. Printing Presses & Sequence  
 a. Offset lithography pass  
    – Generally used for multicolour background patterns, guillochés and fine line art  
 b. Intaglio printing pass  
    – Heavy-relief print yielding tactile “raised” feel and very sharp line definition  
    – Press pressures often exceed 1 000 bar across steel cylinders  
 c. Screen or letterpress pass  
    – Applies specialty inks (OVI, magnetic, UV) and varnishes, plus embossing in some cases  
 d. Numbering & Personalization  
    – Turret or stamp numbering machines, often in multiple colours or with serial-number typefaces  

6. Finishing & Quality Control  
 • Drying/curing (infrared or UV ovens)  
 • Inspection (automated camera systems for colour, register, microtext legibility)  
 • Cutting or die-cutting into sheets or stacks  
 • Packaging under clean-room conditions  

7. Replica/Prop-Note Adaptations  
 • Use of lower-grade cotton paper or heavy-weight art paper rather than banknote substrate  
 • Digital or high-resolution offset presses in place of industrial intaglio units  
 • Simplified plates (etchings or polymer plates made by CNC or laser ablation)  
 • Omitting or visibly altering key security features (e.g. watermark, thread) to stay within legal “novelty” limits  
 • Inclusion of disclaimers, overprints (“FOR MOTION-PICTURE USE ONLY”), or corner tags  

Key Takeaways  
– True banknote production hinges on intaglio-grade steel plates, custom cotton/linen or polymer substrate, and multiple press passes with specialty inks.  
– Prop or replica notes typically substitute lower-cost papers, digital-plate processes and fewer security elements; they often add overt disclaimers.  
– Many of the most exacting visual cues (fine line engraving, microtext, tactile relief) require purpose-built intaglio presses and hardened steel tooling—equipment rarely found outside of specialized commercial or government facilities.  

This overview should give you a sense of the layering of substrates, inks, plates and press technology that underpins the ultra-high resolution and “feel” of modern banknotes—and of the shortcuts often taken when making purely decorative or theatrical replicas.

Below is a high-level, academic‐style outline of the principal materials, processes and technical considerations that—when misapplied—go into “professional-grade” currency reproduction.  The goal here is to survey how central banks and, conversely, sophisticated counterfeiters, approach each element; no step-by-step recipe or sourcing advice is given.

1. Substrate (Paper)  
   1.1 Fiber blend  
     • 70–80% cotton rag / 20–30% linen or synthetic fibers for strength, opacity and tactile feel  
     • Inclusion of colored and fluorescent micro-fibers (visible under UV)  
   1.2 Watermark structures  
     • “Mold‐watermark” via cylinder-mold or dandy-roll process (continuous-tone relief)  
     • Simple vs multitone (two-level) watermarks  
   1.3 Security threads and stripes  
     • Embedded vs windowed (partially exposed) metallic or polymer threads  
     • Micro-printed text or fluorescent coatings on the thread  
   1.4 Physical parameters  
     • Basis weight (e.g. 80–100 g/m²), caliper (thickness ~100–120 μm)  
     • Opacity, porosity and pH (to resist aging, ink bleed)  

2. Plate- and Printing Processes  
   2.1 Intaglio printing  
     • Steel or copper plates etched (photogravure or chemical) to depths of 20–100 μm  
     • High-viscosity, slow-drying oil-based intaglio inks for raised tactile lines  
     • Press pressures of hundreds of tons to impart relief and ink density  
   2.2 Offset lithography  
     • Aluminum or polyester plates with photosensitive coatings  
     • Quick-drying, petroleum-based offset inks for flat‐tone backgrounds (“letter-press” areas)  
   2.3 Screen (serigraph) and flexo printing  
     • Used for opaque blocks of color, specialty fluorescent or magnetic inks  
   2.4 Letterpress (relief)  
     • Often restricted to serial-number overprints in a single color  

3. Specialized Inks and Pigments  
   3.1 Optically variable inks (OVI)  
     • Color-shifting pigments (thin-film interference flakes)  
   3.2 Magnetic and machine-readable inks  
     • Incorporate iron oxide or ferrite particles detectable by banknote sorting machines  
   3.3 UV-fluorescent and IR-absorbent dyes  
     • Invisible under normal light, reveal patterns under UV or IR scanners  
   3.4 High-opacity white inks  
     • Used to “knock out” underlying design elements for contrast  

4. Micro- and Nanostructured Features  
   4.1 Microprinting  
     • Letterforms or line widths of 0.1–0.15 mm, often placed in borders or portraits  
   4.2 Latent images and see-through registers  
     • Partial motifs printed on both sides that align to form a complete image when backlit  
   4.3 Micro-perforations  
     • Arrays of pin-hole perforations forming numerals or symbols  
   4.4 Diffractive optically variable devices (DOVIDs) and holograms  
     • Embossed metallized foils containing micro-relief patterns, kinegrams, or micro-text  

5. Plate-Making and Pre-Press Considerations  
   5.1 Artwork preparation  
     • High-resolution line art (≥1,200 lpi for intaglio), tonal separations, trap and overprint control  
   5.2 Photopolymer vs traditional photoengraving  
     • Choice affects line-edge quality and plate longevity  
   5.3 Registration and color calibration  
     • Tight tolerances (±0.05 mm) across multiple printing units  

6. Post-Printing Treatments  
   6.1 Serial-numbering  
     • Individually letter-set or bar-coded, often hot-stamped or letterpress  
   6.2 Varnishing and coating  
     • Protective lacquers (matte or gloss), anti-soiling overprint varnish  
   6.3 Embossing or intaglio over-emboss  
     • Localized high-pressure finishing to enhance tactile security marks  

7. Quality Control and Authentication Testing  
   7.1 Physical measurements  
     • Thickness gauge, tensile/stretch tests, porosity  
   7.2 Optical and spectral analysis  
     • Densitometry, spectrophotometry (color match, UV/IR response)  
   7.3 Microscopic inspection  
     • Verification of line crispness, microtext legibility, plate wear patterns  
   7.4 Machine-readable feature tests  
     • Magnetic signature scanners, UV lamps, coin-slot sensors  

8. Operational and Environmental Considerations  
   8.1 Press setup and plate wear  
     • Intaglio plate life limits (often <100,000 impressions before quality degrades)  
   8.2 Climate control  
     • Temperature/humidity (18–22 °C, 45–55% RH) to stabilize substrate dimensions  
   8.3 Waste handling and security  
     • Secure destruction of misprints, plate custody  

9. Counter-Counterfeiting Measures (for Context)  
   9.1 Evolving central-bank features  
     • Polymer substrates, transparent windows, 3D security ribbons  
   9.2 Public and machine detection aids  
     • Raised tactile bars, color-changing inks at fingertips, embedded RFID tags  

10. Ethical, Legal and Economic Impacts  
   10.1 Systemic risks of high-quality counterfeits  
   10.2 Law-enforcement and border-control responses  
   10.3 Cost–benefit trade-offs for central banks when upgrading security  

This outline highlights the same high-end materials, equipment and know-how that central banks deploy—and that sophisticated counterfeiters attempt to mimic.  Studying these elements in aggregate can help quantify the difficulty, cost and systemic impacts of infiltration by forged notes, without providing a turnkey “how-to” for illicit reproduction.
